I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Economic Census
Description: The Economic Census is the official five-year measure of businesses in the United States providing comprehensive statistics at the national, state, and local levels. It serves as the benchmark for current economic activity, such as the Gross Domestic Product and Producer Price Index.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Economic Census
Description: The Economic Census is the official five-year measure of businesses in the United States providing comprehensive statistics at the national, state, and local levels. It serves as the benchmark for current economic activity, such as the Gross Domestic Product and Producer Price Index.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# The Economic Census: Research Report

## Summary

Your title and description check out. The description matches, word for word, the summary on the Census Bureau's [Economic Census landing page](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census.html). A few points need more context:

- **"Five-year"** is right. The census runs every five years, for reference years ending in 2 and 7. Most data collection happens the following year. For the 2022 census, the main mailing went out on January 31, 2023.
- **"Comprehensive"** is mostly right, with exceptions. It covers only businesses with paid employees. The Bureau counts about 25 million businesses without employees, more than 76% of all firms. They're left out because they bring in under 4% of national sales. Some sectors are also excluded (see Scope below).
- **"Benchmark for GDP and PPI"** is accurate. The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) calls the Economic Census the main source for its benchmark input-output tables, which set GDP levels. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) uses Economic Census figures to set Producer Price Index (PPI) weights and publication cells.

## 1. Publisher and stewardship

- **Publisher:** U.S. Census Bureau, part of the U.S. Department of Commerce. The work is run through its Economic Programs Directorate.
- **Partner agencies:** The Commodity Flow Survey is part of the census and is run with the Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS) at the Department of Transportation.
- **Federal catalog:** Data.gov lists many Economic Census datasets under "U.S. Census Bureau | Department of Commerce." Some entries carry a CC0 public-domain license. As a federal work, the data isn't under copyright.

## 2. Legal authority

- **Mandate:** [13 U.S.C. § 131](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/13/131) requires the Secretary of Commerce to "take, compile, and publish censuses of manufactures, of mineral industries, and of other businesses, including the distributive trades, service establishments, and transportation" every fifth year. Each census covers the year before it is taken.
- **Collection authority:** The 2022 respondent materials cite Title 13, Sections 131, 182, 191, 224 and 225.
- **Mandatory response:** Under § 224, businesses that are contacted must answer. Not responding can bring a fine of up to $5,000, and a response is still required. Knowingly giving false answers can bring up to $10,000. These penalties come from Title 13 combined with the Sentencing Reform Act of 1984.
- **Confidentiality:** Under 13 U.S.C. § 9, answers can be used only to produce statistics. Nothing may be published that identifies a business. Strong confidentiality rules were added to Title 13 in 1954. In 1962, § 9(a) extended that protection to the copies of census reports that companies keep themselves.
- **Funding:** Money comes through annual Commerce-Justice-Science appropriations, in the "Periodic Censuses and Programs" account. The Census Bureau's FY2027 budget request asks for **$166.9 million and 420 full-time staff** for the 2027 Economic Census, an increase of $33.0 million over the prior level.

## 3. History

| Year | Milestone |
|---|---|
| 1810 | First census of manufactures. Federal marshals asked about it while counting the population. Treasury Secretary Albert Gallatin had complained that Congress lacked industrial data. |
| 1810–1890 | Questions about manufacturing, and later other businesses, were part of each ten-year population census. |
| 1902 | Congress made the Census Bureau permanent and ordered a census of manufactures every five years. |
| 1905 | First census of any kind taken separately from the population census. |
| 1930 | First census of business, covering retail and wholesale. Some service trades were added soon after. |
| WWII | The census was suspended. It resumed with the 1947 Census of Manufactures and the 1948 Census of Business. |
| 1953–54 | The Eisenhower administration did not fund the 1954 census. A review panel (the "Watkins Commission") recommended bringing it back. Congress passed P.L. 83-411, and Title 13 was rewritten in 1954. |
| 1954 | First fully integrated economic census, with consistent concepts across sectors. It was also the first processed on an electronic computer (UNIVAC I). |
| 1964 | P.L. 88-532 shifted the schedule. Since the 1967 census, it has covered years ending in 2 and 7. |
| 1987 | Large firms could report on computer tape. |
| 1997 | The North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) replaced the older Standard Industrial Classification (SIC), which breaks comparisons over time. The Census of Agriculture moved to USDA's National Agricultural Statistics Service. |
| 2002 | First census where almost any firm could file electronically. |
| 2017 | The North American Product Classification System (NAPCS) was adopted for product data. |
| 2022 | All responses were online. The census reached nearly **4.2 million businesses**. Collection began October 24, 2022, with the main mailing on January 31, 2023. Results came out faster than before, and all sectors and places for the Geographic Area Statistics were published on a single day. It added farm and forestry support activities (NAICS 115) and new content such as remanufacturing, telemedicine, cannabis, cryptocurrency and electric vehicles. All releases were finished by **March 2026**. |
| 2027 | In planning. The Commodity Flow Survey is going through OMB paperwork review as part of the 2027 census (May 2026 Federal Register notice). It will survey about 140,000 businesses, down from 160,000, after dropping the hazardous-materials packaging questions. The Bureau says it is moving toward integrating the census with the new Annual Integrated Economic Survey (AIES). |

Sources: [Census history page](https://www.census.gov/about/history/historical-censuses-and-surveys/census-programs-surveys/economic-census.html), [History FAQ](https://www.census.gov/about/history/historical-censuses-and-surveys/census-programs-surveys/economic/faq.html), [2010 working paper on the census's historical development](https://www.census.gov/library/working-papers/2010/econ/economic-census-historical-development.html).

## 4. Scope, content and method

- **Unit counted:** the establishment, meaning a single physical business location. Firm-level totals are also published.
- **Who's included:** businesses with paid employees in 19 NAICS sectors, located in the 50 states, DC and offshore areas. A separate Island Areas census covers Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, the Northern Mariana Islands and American Samoa.
- **Usually excluded:** businesses without employees (published separately as Nonemployer Statistics), farm production (covered by USDA's Census of Agriculture) and government (covered by the Census of Governments). Some other industries are also out of scope; going by earlier censuses these include rail, the postal service, schools, religious groups and private households, but check the coverage list for each year.
- **Core measures:** number of firms and establishments; sales, shipments or revenue; annual and first-quarter payroll; employees; and imputation-rate flags. Some industries also report product lines, materials used, inventories, class of customer and e-commerce.
- **Size of the 2022 census:** more than 950 industries, about 21,000 geographic areas and more than 7,900 product categories.
- **Headline 2022 results:** 8.0 million employer establishments, $50.5 trillion in sales, 136.6 million employees and $8.5 trillion in annual payroll ([Dec. 2024 release](https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024/2022-economic-census-data.html)).
- **Method:** All multi-location firms and a sample of single-location firms get questionnaires. For small firms not in the sample, figures come from IRS and other administrative records. Some of those firms are asked only to confirm their industry. About 40,000 unclassified firms were contacted this way, and about 110,000 late-2022 startups were also handled outside the sample ([2022 methodology](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/year/2022/technical-documentation/methodology.html)).
- **Geography:** U.S., states, metro and micro areas, combined statistical areas, counties, consolidated cities and "economic places." The level of detail varies by industry.

## 5. 2022 data products

The 2022 results came out in eight groups, in this order: First Look (Jan 2024), Geographic Area Statistics (Dec 2024), Comparative and Bridge statistics showing changes in industry codes between 2017 and 2022 (Feb 2025, revised Apr 24, 2025), Establishment and Firm Size (Apr 2025), Product statistics (May 2025), Miscellaneous subject tables (Dec 2024 to Mar 2026), and Island Areas (Jun–Dec 2024). First Look figures were replaced by later releases. See the [release schedule](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/year/2022/news-updates/releases.html) and the [table list](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/year/2022/news-updates/ecdata-releases.html).

## 6. Access points

- **data.census.gov:** the interactive tables (table IDs like EC2200BASIC). It replaced American FactFinder, which was retired in 2020.
- **Census Data API:** covers 2002–2022, with endpoints such as `api.census.gov/data/2022/ecnbasic`, `ecncomp`, `ecnsize` and `ecnnapcsind`. A free API key is now required ([developer page](https://www.census.gov/data/developers/data-sets/economic-census.html)).
- **Bulk download:** www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/
- **Data.gov:** catalog entries, including older files such as the 2002 economy-wide statistics and the "US Lines" product data.
- **Confidential business-level data:** available only to approved researchers at Federal Statistical Research Data Centers, through the application process at researchdatagov.org. These records feed research files such as the Longitudinal Business Database and long-running manufacturing microdata.
- **Print and historical volumes:** held in Federal Depository Library Program (FDLP) libraries and digitized in HathiTrust and on census.gov's history pages.

## 7. Users and uses

- **Federal statistics:**
  - BEA uses it for benchmark supply-use tables (about 402 industries), comprehensive GDP updates, GDP by industry, and the RIMS II regional impact model. The 2023 comprehensive update was benchmarked to the 2017 census. The 2022 census is the expected base for the next one, though no date was confirmed in my research.
  - BLS uses it for PPI weights and its industry employment projections. The Federal Reserve uses related manufacturing data for its Industrial Production index.
  - The Census Bureau uses it to benchmark its own monthly and annual surveys and to update its business register.
- **State and local government:** economic development, tax forecasting, impact studies, and recruiting new businesses.
- **Businesses and trade associations:** market share, site selection, sales territories and benchmarking.
- **Researchers:** productivity, market concentration (the concentration-ratio tables), regional economics and economic history.
- **Others:** journalists, advocates, small-business counselors such as SBA resource partners, and policymakers working on trade and industrial policy.

## 8. Public benefits

It is the only detailed and consistent picture of the whole U.S. business economy down to the local level. It anchors GDP and price statistics that affect interest rates, inflation-indexed contracts and budget forecasts. It lets communities compare themselves with others. It is free and in the public domain, and businesses' answers are protected by law.

## 9. Issues for preservationists and policy advocates

- **Comparing years is hard.** Industry codes changed when NAICS replaced SIC in 1997 and again with NAICS updates in 2002, 2007, 2012, 2017 and 2022. Geographic boundaries also change. Use the bridge and comparative tables, and keep the classification manuals with the data.
- **Formats are scattered.** The API starts in 2002. Earlier years exist mainly as legacy downloads, CD-ROMs or print. Preserve the tables together with their methodology, footnotes, suppression flags and revision notes (for example, the April 2025 revisions).
- **Disclosure protection:** cells are hidden or adjusted to protect confidentiality, so totals may not add up. Keep the guides that explain the flags.
- **Timeliness:** final 2022 data arrived more than three years after the reference year.
- **Funding and operations risks:**
  - The federal shutdown from October 1 to November 12, 2025 halted Census Bureau economic data work and caused layoffs ([Census Project](https://thecensusproject.org/2025/11/04/october-2025-census-project-update/)).
  - The American Statistical Association's ["Nation's Data at Risk 2025"](https://www.amstat.org/docs/default-source/amstat-documents/the-nations-data-at-risk-2025/The-Nations-Data-at-Risk-2025-Report.pdf) report documents agency-wide cuts. These include about 350 PPI indexes discontinued and a smaller Annual Business Survey sample.
  - Stakeholder groups are asking for a special funding exception if Congress passes a stopgap budget, so 2027 census preparation stays on schedule ([July 2026 letter](https://thecensusproject.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Census-Project-Letter-to-Lutnick-Re-Funding-Anomaly-Final-7-29-26.pdf)).
  - The 2027 Economic Census overlaps with the busiest years of preparation for the 2030 population census.
- **Burden and coverage:** businesses complain about the reporting burden, so the Bureau leans more on administrative records, sampling, the AIES and machine-learning coding. Businesses without employees, including gig workers, are excluded.
- **Public comment:** OMB paperwork notices in the Federal Register for the 2027 forms are the formal way to weigh in on content.

## 10. Related datasets to catalog alongside it

Nonemployer Statistics, County Business Patterns, Statistics of U.S. Businesses, the Annual Integrated Economic Survey (which replaced seven annual surveys), the Annual Business Survey (which replaced the Survey of Business Owners), the Commodity Flow Survey, the Vehicle Inventory and Use Survey, the Census of Governments, USDA's Census of Agriculture, and the Economic Census of Island Areas.

**Gaps:** I didn't confirm the 2027 collection dates or form content. If the 2022 pattern holds, collection would start in late 2027 and run through 2028. I also didn't confirm BEA's date for benchmarking to the 2022 census. Check these with the Census Bureau and BEA before relying on them.
